deck.section_name: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry
deck.title: The Periodic Table

front_blocks.md: What is the general trend in first ionisation energy across a period, and why does it occur?

back_blocks.md: First ionisation energy **increases** across a period. Nuclear charge increases while shielding remains roughly constant and atomic radius decreases, making it progressively harder to remove the outer electron.

front_blocks.md: Describe the general trend in melting point across Period 3 (Na to Ar).

back_blocks.md: Melting point **increases** from Na to Si (which has the highest melting point) then **decreases sharply** from P to Ar. The trend reflects changes in bonding and structure across the period.

cards.front_md: Describe the general trend in melting point across Period 3 (Na to Ar).

front_blocks.md: Why is the first ionisation energy of boron lower than that of beryllium, despite boron having a higher nuclear charge?

back_blocks.md: In boron, the outer electron is in the **2p subshell**, which is at a higher energy and further from the nucleus than the 2s subshell of beryllium. This more than offsets the increased nuclear charge, lowering boron's *IE*<sub>1</sub>.

front_blocks.md: Why does the melting point increase from sodium to aluminium across Period 3?

back_blocks.md: Na, Mg and Al have **metallic bonding** in a giant lattice. Going from Na to Al, each atom donates more electrons to the delocalised sea (1, 2 and 3 respectively), increasing the electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the electron sea.

front_blocks.md: The first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen because of **..........**  in oxygen's 2p<sub>x</sub> orbital.

back_blocks.md: The first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen because of **spin-pair repulsion** in oxygen's 2p<sub>x</sub> orbital.
Oxygen has two electrons in 2p<sub>x</sub>; the repulsion makes one of them easier to remove.

front_blocks.md: Silicon has the highest melting point in Period 3 because it has a **..........**  structure.

back_blocks.md: Silicon has the highest melting point in Period 3 because it has a **giant covalent (giant molecular)** structure.
Each Si atom is bonded to four neighbours by strong covalent bonds that require a large amount of energy to break.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
First ionisation energy decreases down a group in the Periodic Table.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

Down a group, atomic radius increases, distance between the nucleus and outer electron increases, and shielding increases. These factors outweigh the increased nuclear charge, making the outer electron easier to remove.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine and argon have low melting points because the covalent bonds within their molecules are weak.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

The covalent bonds within their molecules are strong. It is the weak **instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces** between molecules that require little energy to overcome, giving low melting points.

front_blocks.md: What is **periodicity** in the context of ionisation energy?

back_blocks.md: **Periodicity** is the repeating pattern of chemical and physical properties (including ionisation energy) observed across successive periods of the Periodic Table.

front_blocks.md: What is a **giant metallic lattice**?

back_blocks.md: A **giant metallic lattice** is a regular arrangement of positive metal ions held together by a sea of delocalised electrons. The electrostatic attraction between the ions and the electrons gives metals their high melting points.

cards.back_md: A **giant metallic lattice** is a regular arrangement of positive metal ions held together by a sea of delocalised electrons. The electrostatic attraction between the ions and the electrons gives metals their high melting points.

front_blocks.md: Give three reasons why ionisation energy decreases down a group.

back_blocks.md:
1. **Atomic radius increases** as more electron shells are added.
2. **Distance** from the nucleus to the outer electron increases.
3. **Shielding** by inner electron shells increases.
All three reduce the effective nuclear attraction on the outer electron.

front_blocks.md: Why does sulfur have a higher melting point than phosphorus in Period 3?

back_blocks.md: Sulfur exists as **S**<sub>**8**</sub> molecules, which are larger than the **P**<sub>**4**</sub> molecules of phosphorus. Larger molecules have stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces between them, requiring more energy to overcome.

front_blocks.md: The delocalised electrons in the metallic lattice of aluminium come from the **..........**  shell of each Al atom.

back_blocks.md: The delocalised electrons in the metallic lattice of aluminium come from the **valence** shell of each Al atom.
Aluminium donates all three of its outer electrons to the electron sea.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The decrease in first ionisation energy from phosphorus to sulfur is caused by spin-pair repulsion in sulfur's 3p<sub>x</sub> orbital.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Sulfur has two electrons paired in the 3p<sub>x</sub> orbital. Spin-pair repulsion makes one of these electrons easier to remove than the unpaired 3p electrons in phosphorus.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Argon has a higher melting point than chlorine in Period 3.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Argon exists as single atoms (Ar) with only very weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces, giving it a lower melting point than chlorine (Cl<sub>2</sub>), which has slightly larger molecules and stronger intermolecular forces.

front_blocks.md: Why does increasing nuclear charge not always lead to increasing ionisation energy across a period?

back_blocks.md: Two specific cases cause the general trend to dip: when the outer electron moves to a **higher-energy subshell** (e.g. Be to B, Mg to Al), and when **spin-pair repulsion** in a half-filled orbital makes removal easier (e.g. N to O, P to S).

front_blocks.md: Why do the elements from phosphorus to argon have much lower melting points than silicon in Period 3?

back_blocks.md: Silicon has a giant covalent structure requiring large amounts of energy to break strong covalent bonds. Phosphorus to argon exist as **simple molecules** held together only by weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces, which are easily overcome.
